question.problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)=4xz-{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,1,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,3,2⟩,$ respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)=4xz-{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,3,2⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,3,2)-f(0,1,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,3,2⟩-⟨0,1,1⟩) \\ 3-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ \\ 3 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨4z,-2y,4x+2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨4{c}_{3},-2{c}_{2},4{c}_{1}+2{c}_{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ \\ 3 & =⟨4{c}_{3},-2{c}_{2},4{c}_{1}+2{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ \\ 3 & =4{c}_{3}-4{c}_{2}+4{c}_{1}+2{c}_{3} \\ 3 & =4{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2}+6{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{1} & =\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x & =\frac{y-1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t,\,y=2t+1,\,z=t+1,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t,\,{c}_{2}=2t+1,\,{c}_{3}=t+1.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $3=4{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2}+6{c}_{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4t-4(2t+1)+6(t+1) & =3 \\ 4t-8t-4+6t+6 & =3 \\ 2t & =1 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},{c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =2(\frac{1}{2})+1=2, \\ {c}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}+1=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(\frac{1}{2},2,\frac{3}{2}).$
